title-group.article-title: Retrograde pedal access to facilitate intraluminal recanalization in complex infrainguinal chronic total occlusions

sec.title: Background
sec.p: This study aimed to assess the feasibility, safety, and clinical performance of retrograde pedal access to facilitate intraluminal crossing in complex infrainguinal chronic total occlusions in patients with advanced peripheral artery disease.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: In this retrospective, single-centre analysis, 33 patients undergoing endovascular revascularization for complex peripheral arterial chronic total occlusions between August 2021 and October 2024 were evaluated. Retrograde pedal access was performed when intraluminal crossing could not be achieved using antegrade or contralateral femoral approaches. The primary endpoint was technical success, defined as successful intraluminal crossing. Secondary endpoints included procedural complications, freedom from clinically driven target lesion revascularisation, longitudinal changes in Rutherford classification, wound healing, limb salvage and all-cause mortality.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Successful intraluminal crossing via retrograde pedal access was achieved in 30 patients (90.9%). The posterior tibial artery (39.4%) and anterior tibial artery (36.4%) were the most commonly utilized access sites. Among the 30 patients who underwent definitive endovascular treatment after successful intraluminal crossing, the most frequent complication was flow-limiting dissection, occurring in five patients (16.7%); no cases of perforation, distal embolization, pseudoaneurysm, arteriovenous fistula, or procedure-related death were recorded. Kaplan-Meier estimated freedom from clinically driven target lesion revascularization was 96.7% at 12 months and 75.5% at 24 months. No major amputations occurred, and all patients presenting with tissue loss achieved complete wound healing, with or without minor amputation.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: Retrograde pedal access represents a safe and effective approach for achieving intraluminal crossing in complex peripheral chronic total occlusions, particularly among patients with chronic limb-threatening ischemia. The high rate of technical success and favorable limb-related outcomes support its role as an integral component of modern endovascular revascularization strategies.

body.p: Endovascular revascularization has become the primary treatment strategy for symptomatic peripheral artery disease (PAD) across a broad clinical spectrum, ranging from lifestyle-limiting claudication to chronic limb-threatening ischemia (CLTI).[1] Contemporary guidelines increasingly support an endovascular-first approach in the majority of patients, reflecting advances in device technology, interventional techniques, and peri-procedural management.[2]

Despite these advances, complex infrainguinal chronic total occlusions (CTO) continue to represent some of the most technically challenging lesions in lower extremity endovascular interventions.[3] Long lesion segments, severe calcification, multilevel disease, and inadequate distal targets substantially reduce the likelihood of successful antegrade intraluminal crossing, particularly within the femoropopliteal (FP) and infrapopliteal arterial beds.[4]

To address these challenges, subintimal recanalization techniques have been widely adopted and have improved overall technical success in long and complex CTOs.[5] However, extensive subintimal dissection may disrupt native vessel architecture, compromise collateral branches, and lead to reduced distal run-off. These limitations have become increasingly relevant in the current era of vessel-preserving strategies and drug-coated balloon (DCB) angioplasty, in which preservation of vessel wall integrity and controlled drug delivery are critical determinants of long-term outcomes.[6]

In recent years, retrograde tibiopedal access has emerged as an important adjunctive strategy in the treatment of complex infrainguinal CTOs. By providing direct access to the distal run-off vessels and enabling controlled bidirectional techniques, this approach increases the likelihood of intraluminal crossing, particularly in cases where antegrade attempts have failed.[7]

Beyond technical feasibility, increasing attention has been directed toward the relationship between wire path and clinical outcomes in CTO interventions. Recently published intravascular ultrasound (IVUS)-based data suggest that intraluminal wire passage may be associated with more favourable restenosis-related outcomes compared with subintimal approaches in selected lesion subsets.[8] These findings further support strategies that prioritise true-lumen recanalization.

However, most previous studies have primarily focused on the technical feasibility and safety of retrograde pedal access. Data evaluating its role in facilitating controlled intraluminal recanalization and its impact on mid-term clinical outcomes remain limited. Therefore, the present study aimed to evaluate the safety and effectiveness of retrograde pedal access as an adjunctive strategy for achieving intraluminal crossing in complex infrainguinal CTOs, together with its mid-term clinical outcomes in a real-world population of patients with claudication and CLTI.

sec.title: Study Design
sec.p: This retrospective, single-centre observational study was conducted at a tertiary vascular centre. The study was approved by the Acıbadem Mehmet Ali Aydınlar University Medical Research Evaluation Board (ATADEK) (approval date: 8 January 2026; approval no: 2026-01/21). Consecutive patients who underwent endovascular revascularisation for complex infrainguinal CTOs between August 2021-October 2024 were included in the analysis. During the study period, 132 infrainguinal endovascular procedures were performed, and retrograde pedal access was required in 33 patients (25%). The study flow, including technical success, subsequent management, and clinical follow-up, is summarized in Figure 1.

All patients presented with symptomatic PAD, including both lifestyle-limiting claudication and CLTI. Clinical, demographic, procedural, and follow-up data were collected from institutional electronic medical records. All patients were informed in detail on the treatments and that informed consent was obtained from each patient.

Baseline characteristics including age, sex, cardiovascular risk factors, comorbidities, and clinical presentation were recorded. Lesion characteristics were evaluated angiographically, including lesion location, length, multilevel involvement, and distal run-off status.

sec.title: Endovascular Technique
sec.p: All procedures were performed in a dedicated angiography suite under general anesthesia, with patients in the supine position, according to our institutional practice for complex infrainguinal CTO interventions. General anesthesia was preferred because these procedures frequently required prolonged procedure times, combined antegrade and retrograde arterial access, extensive guidewire manipulation, and repeated balloon inflations. This approach provided optimal patient immobility and procedural comfort, facilitating precise endovascular manipulation throughout the intervention. Continuous hemodynamic monitoring was maintained by the anesthesia team throughout the intervention. The use of general anesthesia reflected our institutional practice and should not be interpreted as a prerequisite for retrograde pedal access, which may also be performed under local anesthesia or conscious sedation according to patient characteristics and institutional preference. Patients who were already receiving dual antiplatelet therapy with aspirin and clopidogrel continued their treatment without interruption, whereas those not on such therapy were initiated on dual antiplatelet treatment at least one week prior to the procedure. After arterial access was obtained, intravenous unfractionated heparin (100 IU/kg) was administered. The activated clotting time (ACT) was first measured approximately 10 minutes after the initial heparin administration. During prolonged procedures, the ACT was monitored periodically, and additional heparin was administered as needed to maintain an ACT >250 seconds throughout the intervention. Following successful revascularization, all patients were prescribed dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin 100 mg/day and clopidogrel 75 mg/day) for 12 months in accordance with the institutional antiplatelet protocol used during the study period. Thereafter, lifelong single antiplatelet therapy, generally with aspirin 100 mg/day, was continued unless contraindicated.

Initial arterial access was obtained via an ipsilateral antegrade or contralateral retrograde common femoral artery approach using 6-7F introducer sheaths, depending on lesion location and operator preference. Diagnostic angiography was performed to assess lesion morphology, occlusion length, distal run-off, and potential target vessels for revascularisation. In all cases, antegrade intraluminal crossing was initially attempted using 0.014- or 0.018-inch guidewires supported by low-profile crossing or support catheters. Antegrade and retrograde crossing of the CTO was performed using 0.014-inch or 0.018-inch guidewires in combination with support catheters to facilitate controlled intraluminal recanalization. Depending on lesion characteristics and operator preference, Navicross® (Terumo, Tokyo, Japan), Rubicon™ Support Catheter (Boston Scientific, Marlborough, MA, USA), and TrailBlazer® Support Catheter (Medtronic, Minneapolis, MN, USA) were used to provide guidewire support during lesion crossing. 0.035-inch guidewires were not used for CTO crossing; however, following successful guidewire externalization, they were selectively exchanged when additional support was required for subsequent antegrade endovascular interventions.

Retrograde pedal access was indicated when antegrade intraluminal guidewire crossing could not be achieved despite conventional guidewire and support-catheter techniques. This strategy was particularly considered in long, calcified, or anatomically complex CTOs in which continued antegrade manipulation was considered unlikely to achieve controlled intraluminal passage. All pedal access procedures were performed using duplex ultrasound guidance with high-frequency linear probes for arterial puncture, with adjunctive fluoroscopic guidance used when necessary for wire advancement and confirmation, based on lesion characteristics and procedural complexity. Depending on vessel anatomy and operator preference, both transverse (out-of-plane) and longitudinal (in-plane) approaches were used. Needle visualization was optimized by maintaining a shallow needle angle and continuous ultrasound monitoring throughout vessel entry. For heavily calcified arteries, puncture was preferentially performed at arterial segments demonstrating the least circumferential calcification on ultrasound, and color Doppler imaging was used to confirm vessel patency and guide the needle trajectory before puncture. In all patients, to minimise distal vessel injury and vasospasm at the access site, arterial puncture was performed using a micropuncture needle, followed by advancement of a support catheter over 0.014- or 0.018-inch guidewires using a sheathless technique.

Following successful pedal access, a retrograde guidewire was carefully advanced toward the occlusion. Initially, soft and torqueable CTO guidewires were used, with gradual escalation in wire stiffness when required. The procedural strategy prioritised intraluminal crossing whenever technically feasible. When necessary, dual-access rendezvous or controlled antegrade and retrograde subintimal tracking (CART)-type techniques were employed to facilitate connection between antegrade and retrograde channels. Particular attention was paid to avoiding uncontrolled subintimal dissection and preserving distal vessel integrity.

After wire externalisation and confirmation of intraluminal position, lesion preparation was performed according to lesion complexity. In non-complex lesions with a low calcific burden, prolonged inflation of plain balloons for approximately 120 seconds was routinely performed to optimize lesion preparation and minimize residual stenosis or flow-limiting dissection before definitive treatment. In contrast, atherectomy or intravascular lithotripsy (IVL) was used in complex and heavily calcified lesions. When DCBs were used, balloon inflation was maintained for approximately 300 seconds according to the manufacturers’ recommendations to maximize drug transfer and tissue uptake. Stent implantation was reserved for cases with flow-limiting dissection or significant elastic recoil.

DCBs were routinely used for FP lesions following successful intraluminal recanalization and adequate lesion preparation unless provisional stenting was required because of significant residual stenosis or flow-limiting dissection. In contrast, DCBs were not used routinely for infrapopliteal interventions because the current evidence supporting their use in below-the-knee (BTK) arteries remains inconclusive. Their use was left to the operator’s discretion and was generally reserved for selected infrapopliteal lesions with a reference vessel diameter of ≥2.5 mm after satisfactory lesion preparation and in the absence of significant residual stenosis, severe recoil, or flow-limiting dissection. Balloon diameter was selected according to the reference vessel diameter and ranged from 2.5 to 4.0 mm.

Retrograde pedal access was used solely to facilitate successful guidewire crossing of the chronic total occlusion. After successful guidewire externalization, iliac interventions, including deployment of self-expanding stents and kissing stents, were performed through retrograde common femoral artery access, which provided appropriate support for the delivery of large-profile devices.

At the end of the procedure, final angiography was performed to confirm adequate inline flow, absence of flow-limiting dissections, and patency of distal run-off vessels. Hemostasis at pedal access sites was achieved by combining balloon angioplasty at the access segment with approximately 180 seconds of external manual compression. Femoral access sites were managed using either manual compression or vascular closure devices, depending on sheath size and access characteristics. All patients were closely monitored post-procedurally for access-site complications and distal limb perfusion.

sec.title: Endpoints and Follow-up
sec.p: The primary endpoint was technical success, defined as successful intraluminal CTO crossing and restoration of inline flow without significant residual stenosis. Secondary endpoints included procedural complications, freedom from clinically driven target lesion revascularisation, wound healing, limb salvage, longitudinal clinical status according to Rutherford classification, and all-cause mortality. Longitudinal clinical deterioration was assessed as time to first recurrence of Rutherford category ≥2 symptoms following successful index revascularization. Only the first clinical recurrence was considered an event.

Patients were routinely followed at 1, 3, 6, and 12 months after the procedure and annually thereafter. Follow-up included clinical examination and duplex ultrasonography. Computed tomography angiography was performed only in patients with recurrent symptoms or when duplex ultrasound suggested restenosis or reocclusion.

sec.title: Statistical Analysis
sec.p: Statistical analyses were performed using IBM SPSS Statistics for Windows, version 27.0 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA). The distribution of continuous variables was assessed using the Shapiro-Wilk test and visual inspection of histograms. Normally distributed continuous variables are presented as mean ± standard deviation, whereas non-normally distributed continuous variables are presented as median with interquartile range and minimum-maximum values. Categorical variables are reported as frequencies and percentages.

Exploratory univariable analyses were performed to identify factors potentially associated with technical success, clinically driven target lesion revascularization (TLR), and procedural complications. Continuous and ordinal variables were compared using the Mann-Whitney U test, while categorical variables were compared using Fisher’s exact test, owing to the limited sample size and the small number of outcome events. Exploratory analyses of clinically driven TLR and procedural complications were restricted to the 30 patients who underwent successful intraluminal crossing and definitive endovascular treatment, whereas the analysis of technical success included the entire study population (n=33).

Freedom from clinically driven TLR and freedom from first recurrence Rutherford category ≥2 symptoms were evaluated using the Kaplan-Meier method. These time-to-event analyses were restricted to the 30 patients in whom successful intraluminal crossing and definitive endovascular treatment were achieved, because only these patients constituted the population at risk for post-treatment TLR and recurrent symptoms. Time zero was defined as the date of the index revascularization procedure. Patients without the respective event were censored at the date of the last available clinical follow-up, and patients who died from causes unrelated to the procedure were censored at the time of death. Kaplan-Meier curves are presented with 95% confidence intervals, censored observations, and numbers at risk.

Because of the relatively small cohort and the limited numbers of technical failures, reinterventions, and procedural complications, multivariable regression analyses were not performed because of the high risk of model overfitting. Therefore, all association analyses should be considered exploratory and hypothesis-generating.
All statistical tests were two-sided, and a p-value <0.05 was considered statistically significant.

sec.title: Patient Characteristics
sec.p: A total of 33 patients were included in the study. The mean age was 66.3±10.5 years, with a median age of 67 years (range: 42-86). The majority of patients were male (78.8%).

Cardiovascular risk factors were highly prevalent. Diabetes mellitus was present in 51.5% of patients, hypertension in 66.7%, hyperlipidemia in 51.5%, and coronary artery disease in 63.6%. Chronic kidney disease was observed in 27.3% of patients, and 12.1% were receiving dialysis. A history of prior coronary revascularisation (CABG or PCI) was present in 42.4% of patients.
Clinically, 60.6% of patients presented with Rutherford category 5 disease, while 27.3% had category 3 and 12.1% had category 4 disease (Table 1).

sec.title: Lesion Characteristics
sec.p: Multilevel disease was common. FP involvement was present in 84.8% of patients, while BTK disease was observed in 90.9%. Iliac involvement was identified in 24.2% of cases. Combined FP and BTK disease was present in 51.5% of patients, and triple-level disease (iliac, FP, and BTK) in 24.2%. In addition, inframalleolar disease was identified in four patients (12.1%).

Lesion lengths reflected high anatomical complexity. The mean lesion length in the superficial femoral artery (SFA) was 212.2±84.9 mm (range 30-350). Infrapopliteal lesions were also long, with mean lengths of 126.9±84.5 mm (range 15-250) in the anterior tibial artery (ATA), 156.7±69.5 mm (range 20-200) in the posterior tibial artery (PTA), and 75.6±55.1 mm (range 20-185) in the peroneal artery (PER) (Table 2).

sec.title: Procedural Characteristics
sec.p: All lesions were CTOs. Retrograde pedal access was most frequently obtained via the PTA (39.4%) (Figure 2) and ATA (36.4%) (Figure 3), followed by the PER (12.1%) (Figure 4). Double retrograde pedal access was required in four patients (12.1%), including two cases via ATA+PTA and two via ATA+PER. Carbon dioxide angiography was used in 21.2% of procedures due to impaired renal function (Table 3).

Five patients with iliac artery disease underwent endovascular intervention, including bilateral common iliac kissing stent grafting (n=1), external iliac artery stenting (n=2), common iliac artery stenting (n=1), and bilateral external iliac DCB angioplasty (n=1). Among 25 patients with SFA disease, 12 were treated with isolated DCB angioplasty, eight with combined atherectomy and DCB angioplasty, and four with stenting alone or in combination with DCB and/or atherectomy. One patient underwent combined IVL and DCB angioplasty. Similarly, among 23 patients with popliteal artery disease, 15 underwent isolated DCB angioplasty, seven received combined atherectomy and DCB angioplasty, and one was treated with IVL and DCB angioplasty.

BTK interventions were performed in multiple arterial segments. Four patients underwent treatment of the tibioperoneal trunk. In the ATA, 15 patients were treated (seven with DCB angioplasty, seven with Plain old balloon angioplasty (POBA), and one with combined atherectomy, DCB, and drug-eluting stent implantation). PTA interventions were performed in eight patients (six POBA, two DCB). In the PER (n=13), seven patients underwent POBA, five DCB angioplasty, and one combined atherectomy and DCB angioplasty.

Four patients had concomitant inframalleolar disease. In these patients, retrograde access was obtained through an appropriate tibial artery rather than an inframalleolar vessel. Following successful retrograde crossing and guidewire externalization, the inframalleolar lesions were crossed antegradely and successfully revascularized using plantar artery balloon angioplasty in three cases and, dorsalis pedis and pedal arch angioplasty in one case. No complications related to the treatment of inframalleolar lesions were observed (Table 4).

sec.title: Procedural Outcomes
sec.p: Successful intraluminal CTO crossing was achieved in 30 patients, corresponding to an overall technical success rate of 90.9%. In the remaining three patients (9.1%), intraluminal crossing could not be achieved despite retrograde attempts.

Among the 30 patients who underwent definitive endovascular treatment following successful intraluminal crossing, flow-limiting dissection occurred in five patients (16.7%). Specifically, dissections were observed in the SFA in three patients, in the proximal ATA in one patient, and in the proximal PER in one patient. Notably, in one of the SFA cases, dissection occurred despite prior atherectomy performed as part of vessel preparation. Dissections involving the ATA and PER were successfully treated with drug-eluting coronary stent implantation, while SFA dissections were managed with self-expandable nitinol stenting.

Acute occlusion occurred in one patient (3.3%), who was among those with SFA dissection. This patient developed a non-flow-limiting dissection at the SFA ostium following DCB angioplasty, which progressed to acute occlusion on the day after the procedure. The patient was successfully treated with thrombolytic therapy followed by SFA stenting. No cases of vessel perforation, distal embolisation, pseudoaneurysm, or arteriovenous fistula were observed, and no procedure-related mortality was recorded (Table 5).

sec.title: Clinical Outcomes
sec.p: The mean follow-up duration was 2.4±0.95 years (median, 2.2 years; IQR, 1.6-3.1 years; range, 1.1-4.2 years). Among the 30 patients with successful revascularization, six patients underwent clinically driven TLR during follow-up because of restenosis or recurrent symptoms. Repeat endovascular interventions were successfully performed at 12, 14, 16, 16, 18, and 22 months after the index procedure. Kaplan-Meier estimated freedom from clinically driven TLR was 96.7% at 12 months and 75.5% at 24 months (Figure 5). All six patients were successfully managed with repeat endovascular intervention.

Among the 20 patients presenting with tissue loss at baseline (Rutherford category 5), complete wound healing was achieved in 12 patients (60%) during follow-up. The remaining eight patients (40%) required minor amputations limited to the toe or forefoot as part of a structured wound management strategy. Importantly, no major amputations occurred, resulting in a 100% limb salvage rate.

During follow-up, nine patients experienced a first recurrence of Rutherford category ≥2 symptoms. In patients who subsequently underwent successful clinically driven reintervention, improvement in Rutherford category after reintervention did not alter their classification as having experienced an event in the time-to-event analysis. Kaplan-Meier estimated freedom from first recurrence of Rutherford category ≥2 symptoms was 93.3% at 12 months and 64.3% at 24 months (Figure 6). The patient who died from a non-procedure-related cause at 25 months was Rutherford category 0 at the time of death and was censored at 25 months without a clinical recurrence event.

Among the 30 patients with successful retrograde pedal recanalization, baseline Rutherford categories were 3 in 9 patients (30.0%), 4 in 3 patients (10.0%), and 5 in 18 patients (60.0%). At final clinical follow-up, Rutherford classification was available for 29 patients because one patient died from a non-procedure-related cause at 25 months while being Rutherford category 0. Of these 29 patients, 23 (79.3%) were classified as Rutherford category 0 and 6 (20.7%) as Rutherford category 2 and were managed conservatively with optimal medical therapy and supervised exercise. No surviving patient remained in Rutherford categories 3-5 at final clinical follow-up (Figure 7).

In the three patients in whom technical success could not be achieved, two presented with CLTI and tissue loss, whereas one had severe claudication due to popliteal artery occlusion following previous trauma. Surgical distal bypass was successfully performed in one patient with CLTI who had a suitable distal PTA target, as well as in the patient with traumatic popliteal artery occlusion without BTK arterial disease. The remaining patient with CLTI had no suitable distal bypass target and was managed with minor amputation, comprehensive wound care, and adjunctive hyperbaric oxygen therapy, ultimately achieving complete wound healing.

One patient (3.3% of the successfully treated cohort) died during follow-up from causes unrelated to the index procedure at 25 months after the intervention. The patient was Rutherford category 0 at the time of death and had experienced neither clinically driven TLR nor recurrent Rutherford category ≥2 symptoms; therefore, the patient was censored at 25 months in both Kaplan-Meier analyses. No deaths were attributable to the endovascular procedure or its complications.

Exploratory univariable analyses were performed to assess factors potentially associated with technical success, clinically driven reintervention, and procedural complications. Multilevel disease was more frequent among patients with technical success than among those with technical failure (83.3% vs. 0%; p=0.010). However, given the very small number of technical failures (n=3), this statistical association should be interpreted with caution and should be considered exploratory and non-conclusive. FP involvement showed a borderline association with technical success (90.0% vs. 33.3%; p=0.053). No other evaluated baseline, anatomical, or procedural variable was significantly associated with technical success (Table 6). No statistically significant associations were identified between the evaluated variables and clinically driven reintervention (Table 7). In the exploratory analysis of procedural complications, coronary artery disease was less frequent among patients with complications than among those without complications (20.0% vs. 76.0%; p=0.031), whereas no other evaluated variable was significantly associated with procedural complications (Table 8). Given the very small number of patients with procedural complications (n=5) and the exploratory nature of these analyses, this finding should be interpreted with caution and considered hypothesis-generating rather than confirmatory. Given the small cohort and the limited number of technical failures, reinterventions, and complications, these analyses should be considered exploratory. Multivariable regression analysis was not performed because of the high risk of model overfitting.

Overall, the combination of high technical success, low complication rates, durable freedom from reintervention, substantial improvement in Rutherford classification, complete limb salvage, and favorable wound healing outcomes highlights the clinical effectiveness and mid-term durability of retrograde pedal access to facilitate intraluminal recanalization in patients with complex PAD and advanced limb ischemia (Table 5).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: The principal finding of the present study is that retrograde pedal access can be effectively integrated into an intraluminal recanalization strategy for complex infrainguinal CTO after failed antegrade crossing. While the technical feasibility and safety of retrograde pedal access have been well established in previous studies, most reports have primarily focused on procedural success and access-related complications rather than longitudinal clinical outcomes. In the present study, retrograde pedal access was associated with a high technical success rate, a low incidence of access-related complications, favorable midterm freedom from TLR, sustained clinical improvement, favorable wound healing, and complete limb salvage. These findings suggest that the value of retrograde pedal access extends beyond obtaining distal access and lies in its ability to facilitate controlled intraluminal guidewire crossing while contributing to durable clinical outcomes in patients with complex infrainguinal disease. This concept is consistent with the evolution of contemporary retrograde techniques from a bailout maneuver to an integral component of complex endovascular revascularization.[9, 10, 11, 12]

Our technical success and safety outcomes are consistent with the growing body of evidence supporting retrograde pedal access in complex infrainguinal CTOs. Early single-center experiences demonstrated that retrograde pedal access substantially increased technical success in complex popliteal and infrapopliteal occlusions while maintaining a low incidence of access-site complications. These findings have subsequently been confirmed by prospective multicenter studies and larger retrospective cohorts reporting technical success rates of approximately 80-90%, even in patients with long lesions, severe calcification, and advanced Rutherford categories.[7, 11, 13, 14, 15] Importantly, our findings further demonstrate that retrograde pedal access should not be viewed merely as a bailout technique for obtaining distal access. Rather, its greatest value lies in facilitating controlled intraluminal guidewire crossing, thereby allowing vessel-preserving endovascular treatment with favorable mid-term clinical outcomes. This concept is further supported by recent IVUS-based evidence demonstrating that true-lumen guidewire passage may be associated with superior restenosis-related outcomes compared with subintimal recanalization.[8]

An important implication of our findings is that retrograde pedal access should not be regarded simply as an alternative access site but rather as a strategic component of contemporary CTO crossing algorithms. In our practice, retrograde pedal access was adopted after unsuccessful antegrade crossing to facilitate controlled intraluminal guidewire passage while minimizing unnecessary subintimal dissection. This approach is particularly relevant in the era of vessel-preserving endovascular therapy, where maintaining native vessel architecture may optimize subsequent treatment with DCBs and reduce the need for bailout stenting.[16, 17] Our favorable mid-term clinical outcomes suggest that an earlier crossover to retrograde pedal access may be reasonable once continued antegrade attempts become ineffective, rather than persisting with repeated subintimal maneuvers. Nevertheless, successful guidewire crossing alone does not determine long-term prognosis. Previous studies have demonstrated that anatomical complexity, run-off quality, and limb threat severity remain major determinants of limb-related outcomes despite technically successful revascularization.[18, 19, 20, 21, 22] Accordingly, retrograde pedal access should be considered an enabling technique within a comprehensive limb salvage strategy rather than an independent predictor of long-term success.

In addition to the international literature, national clinical experience further supports the effectiveness and feasibility of endovascular strategies in peripheral arterial disease. A recent study from Turkish cardiovascular surgery practice demonstrated high technical success rates (93%) and favorable mid-term patency outcomes following endovascular treatment of infrainguinal disease, including complex FP lesions.[23] Similarly, earlier institutional experience with endovascular and hybrid approaches reported high procedural success with low complication rates, emphasizing the importance of a multidisciplinary and hybrid strategy in achieving complete revascularization in multilevel disease.[24] These findings are consistent with our results and further highlight that contemporary endovascular techniques, when combined with appropriate patient selection and operator experience, can be safely and effectively applied across different clinical settings.

Several limitations of this study should be acknowledged. First, the retrospective single-center design and the absence of a comparator group may have introduced selection bias and limit the generalizability of our findings. Second, although exploratory analyses of factors associated with technical success, reintervention, and procedural complications were performed, the relatively small sample size and limited number of events precluded multivariable regression analysis and reduced statistical power; therefore, non-significant findings may also be subject to Type II error. In addition, routine imaging-based surveillance with duplex ultrasonography or computed tomography angiography was not predefined, preventing reliable assessment of primary and secondary patency. IVUS was also not routinely used to confirm intraluminal guidewire position. Finally, all procedures were performed under general anesthesia according to our institutional practice, and therefore this aspect of the treatment protocol may not be directly applicable to centers favoring local anesthesia or conscious sedation. Despite these limitations, the present study reflects real-world practice in patients with highly complex infrainguinal CTOs and provides comprehensive procedural and mid-term clinical outcome data following a standardized intraluminal recanalization strategy.

In conclusion, retrograde pedal access is more than an alternative access technique for failed antegrade recanalization. When integrated into a planned intraluminal crossing strategy, it provides high technical success with a favorable safety profile and encouraging mid-term clinical outcomes in patients with complex infrainguinal CTOs. Our findings support its role as an adjunctive component of contemporary endovascular revascularization and suggest that an earlier transition to retrograde access may facilitate successful lesion crossing while preserving future treatment options. Larger prospective studies with standardized imaging follow-up are warranted to validate these findings.

sec.p: Ethics Committee Approval: The study was approved by the Acıbadem Mehmet Ali Aydınlar University Medical Research Evaluation Board (ATADEK) (approval date: 8 January 2026; approval no: 2026-01/21).

caption.p: Study flow chart. Flow diagram of infrainguinal endovascular procedures, patients requiring retrograde pedal access, technical success, subsequent treatment, and clinical follow-up.

In a patient with chronic limb-threatening ischemia and complete occlusion of all infrapopliteal and inframalleolar arteries, successful intraluminal recanalisation of the posterior tibial artery following retrograde access via the left main plantar artery.

In a patient with chronic limb-threatening ischemia and complete occlusion of all infrapopliteal arteries, antegrade intraluminal crossing of the tibioperoneal trunk and peroneal artery followed by vessel preparation using rotational atherectomy, and subsequent successful intraluminal recanalisation of the anterior tibial artery via retrograde dorsalis pedis artery access.

In a patient with chronic limb-threatening ischemia, presenting with necrotic wounds on the dorsum of the left foot and lateral malleolus, and complete occlusion of all infrapopliteal arteries, successful intraluminal recanalisation of the peroneal artery and tibioperoneal trunk following retrograde peroneal artery access. Clinical appearance of the foot at 18 months after wound care, fourth toe amputation, and skin flap reconstruction.

Distribution of Rutherford categories at baseline and at final clinical follow-up among patients with successful retrograde pedal recanalization. Baseline assessment included 30 patients; final clinical assessment included 29 patients because one patient died from a non-procedure-related cause at 25 months.

table-wrap-foot.p: Values are presented as median (interquartile range) or n (%). The analysis was restricted to the 30 patients with successful intraluminal crossing and definitive endovascular treatment. Procedural complications occurred in five patients, all of whom had flow-limiting dissection; one of these patients also developed acute occlusion on the day after the procedure. Continuous and ordinal variables were compared using the Mann-Whitney U test; categorical variables were compared using Fisher’s exact test. Analyses were exploratory and no adjustment for multiple testing was applied.
